title: THE MAN GOD CHOSE BEFORE ANYONE KNEW HIS NAME
paragraphs: THE MAN GOD CHOSE BEFORE ANYONE KNEW HIS NAME
How an Unknown Craftsman Named Bezalel Revealed a Truth Most Christians Spend a Lifetime Missing
Most people want God to use them.
Few people are willing to be shaped before they are seen.
That is the lesson that ambushed me when I met a man in Scripture whose name appears only briefly, yet whose fingerprints are all over one of the greatest moments in Israel's history.
His name was Bezalel.
Most believers skip past him.
Many sermons barely mention him.
Yet the more I studied his life, the more I realized that Bezalel exposes one of the greatest misconceptions in modern Christianity.
We celebrate platforms.
God celebrates preparation.
We chase visibility.
God develops faithfulness.
We want influence.
God searches for surrender.
And somewhere between our ambition and God's purpose stands a forgotten craftsman whose story still has the power to transform hearts today.
The first time Bezalel appears, God Himself introduces him.
Exodus 31:2-3 says:
"See, I have called by name Bezalel son of Uri, son of Hur, of the tribe of Judah. I have filled him with the Spirit of God, with wisdom, understanding, knowledge, and all kinds of craftsmanship."
The Hebrew text is breathtaking.
The phrase "I have filled him" comes from מָלֵא (male'), meaning to fill completely, to overflow, to occupy fully.
This was not a partial empowerment.
God saturated him.
The text says he was filled with the Spirit of God.
רוּחַ אֱלֹהִים (Ruach Elohim).
The Breath of God.
The Spirit of God.
The active presence of God.
What shocked me is that Bezalel is the first person in Scripture explicitly described as being filled with the Spirit of God.
Not Moses.
Not Joshua.
Not a king.
Not a prophet.
A craftsman.
A builder.
An artisan.
A man whose calling involved tools instead of sermons.
Wood instead of pulpits.
Gold instead of microphones.
Needles instead of stages.
That realization stopped me cold.
Because it reveals something many Christians desperately need to hear.
God is not impressed by titles.
God fills people for assignments.
And the assignment determines the gifting.
Some people have spent years believing they are less important because they are not preachers, worship leaders, missionaries, or public figures.
Bezalel destroys that lie.
The same Spirit that empowered prophets empowered craftsmen.
The same God who called leaders called builders.
The same Lord who anointed speakers anointed creators.
The Kingdom of God has always required both.
Maybe you have spent years wondering whether your work matters to God.
Maybe your office desk does not look spiritual.
Maybe your workshop does not feel holy.
Maybe your business, your art, your writing, your parenting, your craftsmanship, your service, your creativity seem insignificant compared to what others are doing.
Bezalel would understand.
And God would answer.
Your calling becomes sacred when it is surrendered.
The Tabernacle was not merely a building project.
It was the dwelling place of God among His people.
Every curtain.
Every ring.
Every piece of gold.
Every embroidered thread.
Every carved detail.
Every measurement.
Every design.
All pointed toward a greater reality.
Eventually, they would point toward Christ.
The Tabernacle foreshadowed Jesus.
The place where heaven and earth would meet.
The place where God's presence would dwell among humanity.
John writes:
The Greek word is ἐσκήνωσεν (eskēnōsen).
Literally, "tabernacled among us."
Jesus became what the Tabernacle anticipated.
What Bezalel built with his hands pointed toward the Savior who would one day stretch out His hands upon a cross.
Think about that.
An unknown craftsman helped create prophetic imagery that would ultimately glorify Christ centuries later.
Bezalel probably never saw the full impact of his obedience.
Neither will many of us.
That may be one of the hardest lessons in discipleship.
We often want immediate results.
God often works through eternal outcomes.
We want recognition now.
God is writing stories that extend beyond our lifetime.
The Kingdom is filled with people who planted seeds they never saw bloom.
Parents who prayed.
Teachers who invested.
Believers who served quietly.
Grandparents who remained faithful.
Workers who honored Christ in obscurity.
Their names may never trend.
Their reward remains secure.
Jesus never promised earthly fame.
He promised eternal fruit.
There is another detail about Bezalel that pierced my heart.
His name.
בְּצַלְאֵל (Bezalel).
The name literally means "in the shadow of God."
Not in the spotlight.
Not on the throne.
Not at the center of attention.
In the shadow of God.
How different that is from the world we inhabit today.
A culture obsessed with being noticed.
A generation measuring worth by views, likes, followers, and applause.
Yet Scripture presents a man whose greatest identity was simply living under God's shadow.
Psalm 91 echoes this same reality:
"He who dwells in the secret place of the Most High shall abide under the shadow of the Almighty."
The safest place in existence is still the shadow of God.
Not because it is glamorous.
Because it is where grace sustains us.
That truth becomes even more beautiful when viewed through the lens of the Gospel.
Every believer knows what it means to carry failure.
Every believer knows what it means to carry regret.
Every believer has chapters they wish they could rewrite.
Some scandals are public.
Others remain hidden.
Some wounds are visible.
Others bleed in silence.
Yet the story of Scripture is not about perfect people reaching God.
It is about a perfect Savior coming for broken people.
This is why our theme remains so powerful:
The cross is the ultimate evidence.
At Calvary, humanity displayed its worst.
Hatred.
Violence.
Rejection.
Sin.
Yet God transformed history's greatest scandal into history's greatest redemption.
The Greek word for grace is χάρις (charis).
Unmerited favor.
Undeserved kindness.
A gift that cannot be earned.
The Gospel announces that Christ took our shame and exchanged it for His righteousness.
Not because we deserved it.
Because He loved us.
Bezalel reminds us that God delights in taking ordinary lives and using them for extraordinary purposes.
The Gospel reminds us that God delights in taking broken lives and making them new.
Perhaps today you feel overlooked.
Forgotten.
Unqualified.
Invisible.
Bezalel's story whispers hope.
God knows your name before anyone else learns it.
God sees your faithfulness before anyone applauds it.
God prepares people in secret before He uses them in public.
And sometimes He never intends the public stage at all.
Because eternal significance has never depended on earthly visibility.
The lesson I learned from Bezalel is simple, yet life-changing.
The greatest achievement is not being known by people.
It is being known by God.
The greatest platform is not popularity.
It is obedience.
The greatest success is not influence.
It is faithfulness.
And the greatest place a believer can live is exactly where Bezalel lived.
In the shadow of God.
Maybe that is why his story still speaks thousands of years later.
Not because he built something magnificent.
But because God built something magnificent through him.
And perhaps God wants to do the same through you.
Be honest.
Did this expose something you needed to hear?
Your testimony may encourage someone reading beside you who feels unseen today.
The people history forgets are often the people heaven remembers.
